title: Description for selectors for specific input types.
text:
When specifying input types ‘location’, ‘country’, ‘countryRegion’, ‘countryRegionCRS’, ‘CRS’ or ‘crsBbox’, selectors are automatically created that facilitate the selection of those inputs. After being selected, those inputs appear in the input.json of the script or pipeline as objects with various parameters that will be available when loading then in R, Python or Julia.
For example, the ‘location’ selector allows the user to define a bounding box by choosing a country, region and coordinate reference system. Here is an example of an object created through the selection of the Putumayo department in Colombia, in the Bogota 1975 / Colombia West zone reference system:
bbox:
  - 983337
  - 428305
  - 1360903
  - 659616
CRS:
  name: Bogota 1975 / Colombia West zone
  authority: EPSG
  code: 21896
  proj4Def: >-
    +proj=tmerc +lat_0=4.59904722222222 +lon_0=-77.0809166666667 +k=1
    +x_0=1000000 +y_0=1000000 +ellps=intl +towgs84=307,304,-318,0,0,0,0 +units=m
    +no_defs +type=crs
  unit: metre
  bbox:
    - -79.1
    - 0.03
    - -75.58
    - 10.21
country:
  englishName: Colombia
  ISO3: COL
region:
  regionName: Putumayo Department
  regionGID: COL.24_2
  countryEnglishName: Colombia
Here is the meaning of each key.








Key name
Section
Description




bbox
bbox
Array containing the minimum x, minimum y, maximum x, maximum y coordinates (in that order) of the bounding box, in units of the selected CRS.


name
CRS
Plain text name of the coordinate reference system selected.


authority
CRS
Authority associated with the code of the reference system. Usually EPSG or ESRI. For example EPSG` for ‘EPSG:4326’.


code
CRS
Code associated with the authority of the reference system. Usually a 4 or 5 digit integer. For example 4326`for EPSG:4326


proj4Def
CRS
Proj4 string definition of the CRS.


wktDef
CRS
Well Known text definition of the CRS, when available.


unit
CRS
units associated with CRS. Usually meter, degree, or feet


CRSBboxWGS84
CRS
The bounding box covered by this coordinate reference system, in latitude, longitude, WGS84 (EPSG:4326)


englishName
country
English name of the selected country, according to GADM.org.


ISO3
country
3 letter ISO code for this


regionGID
region
Identifier of the region in GADM


countryEnglishName
region
English name of the country within which this region is.



When using other selectors, the object create contains a subset of the location selector. For example, the countryRegion selector will only contain the country and region sections, and countryRegionCRS will contain all but the bbox section.

title: Peer review
text:
To ensure that analytical pipelines available through the Biodiversity Evaluation Engine (BEE) are scientifically robust, reproducible, and accessible, BON in a Box has established a peer-review process for contributed pipelines.
The review process evaluates the scientific methodology, technical functionality, generalizability, documentation, and usability of each pipeline. It also provides an opportunity for researchers and practitioners to contribute their expertise to improving the tools available through BEE.
Pipelines are typically reviewed by 2–5 experts with complementary scientific, technical, or practical expertise. Where possible, we aim to include reviewers from both the academic and biodiversity monitoring or policy communities.

title: Peer review
section: When is a pipeline ready for peer review?
text:
When is a pipeline ready for peer review?
Before a pipeline is submitted for external review, the BON in a Box team works with contributors to ensure that it:

Meets the requirements outlined in the Pipeline Standards.
Runs successfully using the provided example inputs and default parameters.
Has undergone initial testing with different input data, parameters, and geographical contexts, where applicable.
Produces scientifically reasonable results consistent with the underlying methodology.
Includes input and output descriptions, documentation, and a workflow description.
Has its code available in the BON in a Box GitHub repository, either in the main branch or in a development branch or pull request.

The BON in a Box team conducts initial testing and technical checks before inviting external reviewers. External reviewers are then asked to conduct additional, independent testing to evaluate the pipeline’s functionality, scientific validity, and applicability across different contexts.

title: Peer review
section: How does the peer-review process work?
text:
How does the peer-review process work?

1. Reviewer selection
The pipeline contributor may suggest potential reviewers with relevant expertise. Additional reviewers will be identified by the BON in a Box team and GEO BON network.
We aim to select reviewers with complementary expertise across three areas:







Preferred reviewer type
Primary areas of expertise




Scientific expert
Scientific methodology, assumptions, validation, and interpretation of results


Applied biodiversity monitoring expert
Generalizability, usability, and relevance to biodiversity monitoring, conservation planning, and reporting


Technical expert
Code quality, reproducibility, data handling, and pipeline functionality



These categories are intended to guide reviewer selection rather than establish rigid roles. Reviewers may have expertise in multiple areas, and are not expected to evaluate aspects outside their expertise.
Reviewers are invited by the BON in a Box team and provided with the materials needed to evaluate the pipeline.


2. Pipeline evaluation
Reviewers are asked to evaluate the pipeline using a standardized review form, focusing on the following criteria:

Scientific rigor: Is the methodology scientifically supported and correctly implemented? Are the assumptions and limitations clearly communicated?
Generalizability: Can the pipeline be applied across different geographical areas, species, ecosystems, or scales, where appropriate?
Functionality: Does the pipeline run successfully and produce the expected outputs?
Data use: Are input datasets appropriate, accessible, and clearly documented? Can users provide their own data where relevant?
Usability: Are the inputs, parameters, and outputs understandable to users without extensive programming experience?
Documentation: Are the methodology, inputs, outputs, and interpretation of results adequately explained?
Code quality: Is the code readable, modular, reproducible, and appropriately documented?

Reviewers are encouraged to focus on the criteria most relevant to their expertise. They do not need to complete every section of the review form, but should provide sufficient feedback to support an assessment of the pipeline.


3. Review feedback and revisions
Reviewers submit their completed review forms to the BON in a Box team, including identified issues, recommendations, and an overall assessment of the pipeline.
The completed review forms serve as the formal record of the review. The BON in a Box team consolidates feedback and works with pipeline contributors to address reviewer comments.
Specific technical changes, bugs, and requested improvements are tracked through GitHub issues or pull-request comments, allowing contributors and the BON in a Box team to document and monitor revisions.
Depending on the extent of the revisions required, reviewers may be invited to reassess the pipeline before a final decision is made.


4. Review outcome
Following the review, a pipeline may be:

Accepted with minor revisions: The pipeline meets the main scientific and technical requirements, with only minor changes needed before publication.
Revisions required: More substantial changes are needed, and the pipeline will require additional review.
Not accepted: The pipeline does not currently meet the requirements for inclusion in BEE.

The BON in a Box team coordinates the final decision based on reviewer feedback and the Pipeline Standards.

title: Peer review
text:
Instructions for reviewers
Reviewers will receive a pipeline-specific review form containing the information and resources needed to complete their evaluation, including:

Instructions for accessing the pipeline through the online BEE platform.
Links to the relevant GitHub repository, branch, pull request, or source files.
Links to the pipeline description and supporting scientific documentation.
Any additional information or example datasets relevant to the review.

Pipelines undergoing review will be available through the online BEE platform, so reviewers do not need to install BEE locally. The corresponding source code will be publicly accessible through GitHub, including pipelines that have not yet been merged into the main branch.

Step 1. Access BEE
Reviewers can access BEE through the online platform.
If you do not already have access, create a free GEO BON account and follow the access instructions provided in your review form.


Step 2. Run the pipeline
Locate the pipeline identified in your review form and run it using the provided example inputs and default parameters.
Although the pipeline will have undergone initial testing by the BON in a Box team, reviewers are asked to independently verify that it runs successfully, produces the expected outputs, and provides clear input and output descriptions.


Step 3. Evaluate the methodology and documentation
Review the pipeline description and relevant scientific references.
Consider whether the methodology is appropriate, whether its assumptions and limitations are clearly explained, and whether the outputs are consistent with the intended application.


Step 4. Test different inputs and parameters
Where possible, run the pipeline with different parameters, geographical areas, or datasets.
We encourage reviewers to test the pipeline using data or study areas they are familiar with, as this can help identify unexpected results or methodological limitations that may not have been identified during initial testing.
Document any errors, unexpected behaviour, or concerns in the review form.


Step 5. Review the code (where applicable)
Reviewers with relevant programming experience are encouraged to examine the source code using the GitHub links provided in the review form.
Code review may include checking the implementation of the scientific methodology, reproducibility, modularity, and error handling.
Specific technical issues can be documented in the review form or raised directly through comments on the relevant GitHub pull request.


Step 6. Submit your review
Complete the relevant sections of the review form, including your assessment of the pipeline, any recommended changes, and your overall recommendation.
Reviewers are encouraged to provide detailed feedback within their areas of expertise but are not required to assess every aspect of the pipeline.
Return the completed form to the BON in a Box team using the instructions provided with your review invitation.

title: About
text:
BON in a Box is an initiative of the Group on Earth Observations Biodiversity Observation Network (GEO BON) that brings together scientific expertise, tools, and biodiversity analysis to support biodiversity monitoring and reporting.
The platform provides resources for developing Biodiversity Observation Networks (BONs), a catalogue of biodiversity monitoring projects and tools, and the Biodiversity Evaluation Engine (BEE), which enables users to calculate Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs) and biodiversity indicators.
For more information about BON in a Box in general, please refer to BON in a Box’s website. For more details on the rationale supporting the pipeline engine, refer to our BioScience publication.

What is BON in a Box’s Biodiversity Evaluation Engine (BEE)?
The Biodiversity Evaluation Engine (BEE) is an open-source platformx that brings together biodiversity data and scientific methods to calculate EBVs and indicators for biodiversity monitoring, conservation planning, and reporting.
BEE makes scientific analyses more accessible by allowing users to run standardized and reproducible analytical workflows without needing to develop the underlying code themselves. These automated workflows are called pipelines.
Developed through contributions by the GEO BON scientific community, BEE integrates scientific expertise and methods from researchers around the world, enabling users to:

Calculate biodiversity indicators and EBVs using scientifically robust and transparent methods.
Integrate diverse data sources, including local biodiversity observations, global datasets, and Earth observation data.
Run reproducible analyses through standardized workflows that can be applied across different geographical areas and contexts.
Access and contribute scientific methods through an open-source, community-driven platform.

BEE supports biodiversity monitoring at local, national, and global scales, including the calculation of indicators relevant to the Kunming–Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF).


Why do we need this platform?
Scientists around the world are developing tools to create workflows to calculate Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs) and indicators to report on biodiversity change. However, these initiatives happen in parallel, leading to duplication of effort. BON in a Box allows networks to re-use and enhance each other’s work, by providing a platform to share workflows and tools.
At the same time, countries and organizations responsible for biodiversity monitoring and reporting may lack the technical resources or expertise needed to implement these methods.
BEE aims to bridge the gap between scientific research and its practical application in biodiversity monitoring and decision-making.
By bringing together analytical methods in a shared, open-source platform, BEE reduces duplication of effort, promotes scientific collaboration, and makes biodiversity analyses more accessible to a broader range of users.


From biodiversity data to decision making
BEE connects biodiversity data with scientific methods to generate outputs that can inform conservation planning, biodiversity monitoring, and reporting.
Users can combine their own data with publicly available datasets, including species occurrences, protected areas, environmental variables, and Earth observation products.
These data are processed through automated analytical pipelines to produce outputs such as species distribution maps, connectivity metrics, EBVs, and biodiversity indicators.
By providing transparent and reproducible methods, BEE supports consistent biodiversity assessments across regions and over time, while allowing users to incorporate data and information relevant to their local context.


What is a pipeline?
A pipeline is an automated sequence of analytical steps that transforms input data into meaningful outputs for biodiversity monitoring and decision-making.
Each pipeline brings together smaller, reusable components called scripts, which perform specific tasks such as downloading data, cleaning observations, running statistical models, or generating spatial outputs.
These scripts can be combined and reused across different pipelines, making it easier to develop new analyses and adapt existing methods.
If a pipeline builds upon the results of another pipeline, this “inner pipeline” can be included as a step in the “outer pipeline”; we call this a subpipeline. An SDM pipeline could serve to generate range maps inside a Species Habitat Index pipeline, or embedded in a Species Richness pipeline. We can thus define a step as “a script or a subpipeline performing an operation in the context of a pipeline”.
BEE supports workflows developed in multiple programming languages, including R, Python, and Julia, allowing methods from different scientific communities to be integrated into a common analytical framework.



Simplified pipeline with steps (blue), intermediate results (grey), and final results (green)




Why should you contribute?
BON in a Box is built on collaboration across the global biodiversity research and monitoring community.
Researchers and developers can contribute analytical pipelines, scientific methods, and improvements to existing workflows, helping make their research accessible and applicable beyond its original context.
Contributing to BEE can help:

Increase the impact of research by making scientific methods available for biodiversity monitoring and conservation decision-making.
Promote reproducibility and transparency through open-source, documented workflows.
Support collaboration by allowing researchers to build on and improve existing methods.
Strengthen biodiversity monitoring capacity by making analytical tools more accessible to organizations and countries.

Contributed pipelines follow documented quality standards, with peer review supporting the scientific robustness, usability, and generalizability of published workflows.
To learn more, see our contribution guidelines and peer-review process.


How to cite
Please cite the BON in a Box platform as:
Jory Griffith, Jean-Michel Lord, Michael D Catchen, Maria Isabel Arce-Plata, F Guillaume Blanchet, Mathusan Chandramohan, M Camila Diaz-Corzo, Dominique Gravel, César Gutiérrez, Isabelle S Helfenstein, Sean Hoban, Jamie M Kass, Linda Laikre, Guillaume Larocque, Deborah M Leigh, Brian Leung, Alicia Mastretta-Yanes, Katie L Millette, Maria Alejandra Molina Berbeo, Dat Nguyen, Kari E Norman, María Helena Olaya-Rodríguez, Simon Pahls, Kaitlyn Pereira, Pedro R Peres-Neto, Timothée Poisot, Laura J Pollock, Juan Carlos Rey-Velasco, Victor J Rincon-Parra, Claudia Roeoesli, François Rousseu, Lina María Sánchez-Clavijo, Meredith C Schuman, Oliver Selmoni, Jessica M da Silva, Erika Suarez-Valencia, Thilina D Surasinghe, Eren Turak, Luis Fernando Urbina, Sarah Valentin, Noah Wightman, Juan Zuloaga, Maria Cecilia Londoño, Andrew Gonzalez, BON in a Box: An Open and Collaborative Platform for Biodiversity Monitoring, Indicator Calculation, and Reporting, BioScience, 2026, biaf189, https://doi.org/10.1093/biosci/biaf189
Where applicable, users should also cite the individual analytical pipeline and its associated scientific methodology.

title: Install
section: Deploying the Biodiversity Evaluation Engine (BEE) locally
text:
Deploying the Biodiversity Evaluation Engine (BEE) locally
BEE can be installed and ran on a local computer. While personal computers have less computing power than servers, it is more convenient for pipeline development, or when working with small examples. Users adding scripts and creating pipelines on their local computer can run them directly through BEE in the user interface.
Prerequisites:

A GitHub account, and git installed on your computer
At least 6GB of free space (RAM requirements depend on the script that is being run)
A Linux shell

This can be Terminal on a Mac or Git Bash on a PC



Step 1: Install Docker

Install Docker here

Note: It is not necessary to make an account
To test whether docker is added to the path of your terminal, run docker run --rm hello-world
For Mac users: Make sure to check the chip of your machine and download the correct version.

If there is an error message when running docker run --rm hello-world, see https://stackoverflow.com/a/71923962/3519951
If you encounter error no matching manifest for linux/arm64/v8 in the manifest list entries, export DOCKER_DEFAULT_PLATFORM. See https://stackoverflow.com/a/76404045/3519951.
If you have a Silicon chip, check “Use Rosetta for x86_64/amd64 emulation on Apple Silicon” in the Docker Desktop preferences. See issue #175.

For Linux users: Make sure to add your user to the docker group




Step 2: Generate SSH Key

First, make sure that you do not already have an SSH key registered to your computer by running ls -al ~/.ssh in your terminal.

If you already have a key it will be called one of the following:

id_rsa.pub
id_ecdsa.pub
id_ed25519.pub


If you do not already have a key, generate one by running ssh-keygen -t ed25519 -C "your_email@example.com" replacing the email with the email address associated with your GitHub account.

This will prompt you to make a passphrase. If you choose to have a passphrase, although more secure, it will prompt you to enter it many times while creating a pipeline so consider skipping this step for easier use. You can keep pressing enter to continue without creating a passphrase.

To check if you successfully generated the SSH key, you can run ls -al ~/.ssh in the terminal. Your SSH key should be there now.
Now, open the file with your SSH key by running cat ~/.ssh/<name of SSH key> e.g. cat ~/.ssh/id_ed25519.pub and copy your SSH key.
Now, add your SSH key to your GitHub account by going to GitHub settings > SSH and GPG keys and “New SSH key”. You can name this whatever you want and paste your SSH key into the “Key” field.



Step 3: Clone repository

Choose a folder outside any cloud backup system.
Windows users: make sure the cloned repo is under the user folder (for example C:\Users\yourname\bon-in-a-box), and not under OneDrive.
Mac users: make sure the cloned repo is under the user folder (for example ~/bon-in-a-box), and not under iCloud.
Clone the repository either via terminal using git clone --config core.autocrlf=false git@github.com:GEO-BON/bon-in-a-box-pipelines.git or in GitHub desktop.
Windows users only: if using github desktop to clone, you will have to do these extra steps in the console after cloning to avoid problems with the CRLF line endings:

cd to the cloned folder’s root directory (for example cd /c/Users/yourUsername/folder/bon-in-a-box-pipelines)
git config core.autocrlf false
git rm --cached -r .
git reset --hard




Step 4: Set environment file

Provide the environment variables: Open the newly cloned repository on your computer

Find the file called runner-sample.env
Duplicate the file and rename the copy to runner.env.
Fill the properties depending on what you intend to run. Include any API keys that you need to access data (e.g. GBIF or IUCN)
Adjust any server option as you see fit (optional).

Using a Linux terminal (terminal on Mac, Git Bash or WSL on Windows), navigate to the folder of the cloned repository.
If you are not in the same folder as the cloned repository, navigate to that folder so it can access the files. This can be done with `cd <folder name>`

On Windows, the drives will be noted as /c/ instead of C:\. The path should look like
` /c/Users/yourUsername/folder/bon-in-a-box-pipelines`

In the Linux terminal, type ./server-up.sh

Note for windows users: this has to be a Linux terminal (e.g. git bash). Launching the server locally will not work using Powershell or Windows CMD terminal.
If using Docker Desktop, make sure you have docker open and running on your computer.
The first execution will be long, in order to download the micro-services. The next ones will be shorter or immediate, depending on the changes.
Network problems may cause the process to fail. First try running the command again. Intermediate states are saved so not everything will be redone even when there is a failure.
Windows users may need to turn on virtualization and other tools for Docker Desktop to work and update wsl (“wsl –update”, see https://docs.docker.com/desktop/troubleshoot/topics/#virtualization). Access to the BIOS may be required to enable virtualization.

The startup script might prompt you for an update. Accepting it is recommended.



Step 5: Opening BEE in the browser

In a regular browser, type http://localhost/ to open BEE
Head to the ““Run a Pipeline” and select the one that interests you. See Running a script or pipeline section.



Step 6: Stopping BEE

Run ./server-down.sh in the terminal to stop the server when done
On Windows, to completely stop the processes, you might have to run wsl --shutdown



Updating BEE
Each time that the server is started, the startup script will check for updates and propose them. Type y for yes or press enter to update.
Accepting the updates are generally recommended, unless:

You are currently using an unstable, rate-limited, or billable Internet connection. Defer the update by typing n (no) until a better internet connection is available. You can also use ./server-up.sh --offline option to completely skip update checks. Use with caution, since this may create errors if elements of the repository depend on new server features.
The runner containers need to be discarded, and you are using a pipeline that has installed dependencies. This is the case for a minority of script whose dependencies cannot be found on anaconda.org. Since we know that installing dependencies live can take a while, when the runners need an update, you will see a warning like this:

In this case, defer the update until you can afford the time to start a run that will reinstall the dependencies.

title: Install
section: Deploying BON in a Box on a server
text:
Deploying BON in a Box on a server
Installation steps on a server are the same as installing on a Linux computer, but some additional configurations need to be changed.
In runner.env:

Choose the appropriate HTTP_ADDRESS and HTTP_PORT for your server configuration. In a typical installation, use 0.0.0.0 as an HTTP address and default port (80).
Set SCRIPT_SERVER_CACHE_CLEANER=partial. This will allow for calculated results to be long-lived on the server, as long as they are not run again with a new version of the script. The results in the output folder are always accessible by URL.
To prevent users to modify the pipelines, set SAVE_PIPELINE_TO_SERVER=deny
It is recommended to use a captcha on public-facing servers. Add your keys for Google’s repatcha.
In the case where a server is used for demonstration purposes only, set environment variable BLOCK_RUNS=true
Configure the “Cloud-scaling” section if you have access to a kubernetes cluster. This is still experimental.
Connecting to a High-Performance Computer (HPC) is still experimental. Refer to the developer documentation for guidance and limitations.

Server setup:

The outputs are precious, while the server machine can be re-generated anytime. Consider mounting an external backed-up drive to the output folder of your BEE installation.
By default, BEE listens for http. To enable https, we hide it behind a reverse proxy (documentation here) and activate https with certbot (documentation here).

title: Contributing
text:
BON in a Box is a community-driven initiative that brings together scientific methods and expertise to support biodiversity monitoring and reporting.
We welcome contributions from researchers, developers, and organizations interested in making biodiversity analyses more accessible, reproducible, and widely applicable.
By contributing to the Biodiversity Evaluation Engine (BEE), you can help translate scientific research into practical tools that support biodiversity monitoring, conservation planning, and policy reporting.

title: Contributing
text:
Why contribute?
Researchers around the world are developing methods to assess biodiversity change, but these methods are often difficult to access or apply beyond their original research context.
Contributing to BON in a Box helps make these methods available to a broader community while supporting open science, reproducibility, and collaboration.
Contributors can:

Increase the impact of their research by making analytical methods accessible to researchers, practitioners, and decision-makers.
Support reproducible science by sharing transparent, standardized analytical workflows.
Collaborate with the GEO BON community to improve and expand existing methods.
Support biodiversity monitoring and reporting by helping countries and organizations calculate Essential Biodiversity Variables (EBVs) and biodiversity indicators.

title: Contributing
text:
What can you contribute?
We welcome several types of contributions, including:

New analytical pipelines: Methods for calculating EBVs, biodiversity indicators, or other metrics relevant to biodiversity monitoring.
Improvements to existing pipelines: Updates to scientific methods, additional functionality, new data sources, or improvements to performance and usability.
Individual scripts and technical contributions: Reusable components, bug fixes, and improvements to the underlying platform.
Documentation and testing: Improvements that make BEE easier to understand, use, and maintain.


Is your analysis pipeline a good fit?
We are particularly interested in pipelines that:

Calculate biodiversity metrics relevant to monitoring, conservation planning, and policy reporting.
Are open source and developed using supported programming languages, such as R, Python, or Julia.
Can be applied across different species, countries, regions, or monitoring contexts.
Can be automated and reproduced using clearly defined inputs, analytical steps, and outputs.

Pipelines do not need to be fully developed or meet all technical requirements before you contact us. The BON in a Box team can help assess whether a proposed contribution is suitable and identify what may be needed for integration.
For more details, see our Pipeline Standards.

title: Contributing
text:
How to contribute a pipeline
We encourage contributors to get in touch early in the development process so that we can work together to make pipelines reusable, reproducible, and compatible with BEE.

Step 1. Get in touch
Contact the BON in a Box team at boninabox@geobon.org to discuss your proposed contribution.
We can help determine whether your method is a good fit, identify existing components that could be reused, and discuss the resources and technical support needed for integration.


Step 2. Design your pipeline
Develop a high-level overview of the analytical workflow, including its inputs, processing steps, and expected outputs.
The BON in a Box team can help identify opportunities to make the pipeline modular, generalizable, and compatible with existing BEE components.
We recommend starting with a simple, functional version before adding more complex features.


Step 3. Develop and test
Develop your pipeline following the Pipeline Standards, which outline requirements for documentation, reproducibility, usability, and technical integration.
Contributors can work with the BON in a Box team to test their pipelines and ensure they function correctly within BEE.


Step 4. Peer review
Once a pipeline is complete and meets the required standards, it can be submitted for peer review.
The review process evaluates the scientific methodology, reproducibility, documentation, and usability of the pipeline.
Contributors may be asked to make revisions based on reviewer feedback before the pipeline is accepted.
For more information, see our Peer Review Process.


Step 5. Publication and continued development
Once accepted, the pipeline can be published through BON in a Box and made available for use by the wider community.
Published pipelines can receive a DOI, allowing the contribution to be identified and cited.
Contributors are encouraged to continue improving their pipelines as new methods, datasets, and scientific knowledge become available.

title: Contributing
text:
Other ways to contribute
You do not need to develop a complete analytical pipeline to contribute to BON in a Box.
We also welcome contributions to existing pipelines, documentation, testing, and software development.
You can explore our open-source repositories on the GEO BON GitHub organization or contact the team to discuss opportunities to contribute.

title: Contributing
text:
Interested in contributing?
Whether you have an existing analytical method, an idea for a new pipeline, or would like to support the development of BEE, we would be happy to hear from you.
Contact us at boninabox@geobon.org to discuss your contribution.

title: Instructions for adapting your code to an analysis pipeline
text:
This guide provides step-by-step instructions for adapting an existing analytical workflow or developing a new pipeline for the Biodiversity Evaluation Engine (BEE).
BEE supports pipelines developed in R, Python, Julia, and other supported languages. Pipelines are built from individual scripts that can be connected to create reproducible analytical workflows.
The instructions below will guide you through preparing your code, defining inputs and outputs, building and testing your pipeline, and submitting it for review.
New to contributing? We recommend first reading our Contributing page for an overview of the contribution process and our Pipeline Standards for the scientific and technical requirements.

title: Instructions for adapting your code to an analysis pipeline
text:
Before you start
To develop and test pipelines, you will need:

A GitHub account: Contributions are managed through the BON in a Box pipelines repository.
A local installation of BEE: Follow the Installation Guide to set up the platform on your computer.
An analytical workflow: This can be an existing script or a new method you would like to develop into a pipeline.
A code editor: Such as Visual Studio Code or RStudio, to develop and modify your scripts.

Before beginning development, we recommend contacting the BON in a Box team to discuss your proposed pipeline and identify opportunities to reuse existing components.

title: Instructions for adapting your code to an analysis pipeline
text:
General GitHub contribution workflow
Contributors will follow the GitHub flow when contributing pipelines to BON in a Box. Contributors can follow these steps:

Make sure you have a personal/institutional GitHub repository.
If BON in a Box developers have granted you access to the repository, create a branch for your pipeline. Otherwise, fork the bon-in-a-box-pipelines repository to your personal GitHub repository and then clone it to your computer.

Documentation on working with forks can be found here and cloning here.
Make sure you keep the forked repository up to date by adding the bon-in-a-box-pipelines repository as an upstream repository and regularly fetching changes.

Create a branch from the main branch for your pipeline, with a descriptive branch name (e.g. ProtConn_pipeline).
Create your pipeline on this branch. Make sure it adheres to the pipeline standards.
When it is complete, create a pull request (instructions here) to the main branch on the bon-in-a-box-pipelines GitHub and fill out the peer review template that will autofill in the pull request, suggesting at least two potential peer reviewers.
When peer review is complete, make any suggested changes to the pipeline and resubmit.
When the pipeline has been accepted, it will be merged to the main branch and published on Zenodo with a DOI.
The BON in a Box team will contact you for any bug fixes or feature requests, and new releases will follow the versioning structure specified at the bottom of this page.
During the development process of the pipeline, regularly merge the main branch to your branch to avoid potential conflicts when merging your branch.

How to create a pipeline video tutorial

Analysis workflows can be adapted to BON in a Box pipelines using a few simple steps. Once BON in a Box is installed on your computer, pipelines can be edited and run locally by creating files in your local BON-in-a-box folder cloned from the GitHub repository. Workflows can be written in a variety of languages, including R, Julia, and Python, and not all pipeline steps need to be in the same language.

title: Instructions for adapting your code to an analysis pipeline
text:
Step 1: Plan your pipeline
The first step is to sketch out what your pipeline will look like. This includes breaking up your workflow into logical steps that perform one task and could potentially be reused in other pipelines. Think of the inputs and outputs that you want each script to have and how you want to connect these into a full pipeline.
Here is an example:

Check if any of the steps you need are already available in BON in a Box to avoid having to rewrite them.

title: Instructions for adapting your code to an analysis pipeline
text:
Step 2: Break up your scripts
You can start writing the individual scripts in your pipeline. If you already have an analysis workflow, break this up into individual scripts representing the steps of the pipeline. Plan what you want as the inputs and outputs for each script.

title: Instructions for adapting your code to an analysis pipeline
text:
Step 3: Create a YAML file
Each script should be accompanied by a YAML file (.yml extension) that specifies inputs and outputs of that step of the pipeline.
Markdown is supported for pipeline, script, input, and output descriptions. See this CommonMark quick reference for allowed markups. These can include special characters, links, and images.

Name and description
YAML files should begin with a name, description, and the authors of the script. The name should be the name of the script described by the YAML file (script_name.R below). Save the file with the same name as the script that it describes but with a .yml extension (e.g. if the script is called my_script.R the YAML should be called my_script.yml).
Example:
script: script_name.R
name: Script Name
description: Describe what the script does
author:
  - name: John Doe (john.doe@gmail.com)
  - name: Jane Doe (jane.doe@gmail.com)


Inputs
Next, the YAML file should specify the inputs of the script. These inputs will either be outputs from the previous script, which can be connected by lines in the pipeline editor, or specified by the user in the input form.
All input and output ids should follow the snake case naming conventions. Names should be all lowercase with underscores instead of spaces. For example, an input labelled “Species name” would have the snake case id of “species_name”. This id will be the name of the input parameter in your code.
Here is an example where the inputs are a coordinate reference system and a distance, specified by the user:
inputs:
  crs:
    label: coordinate reference system for output
    description: ESPG coordinate reference system for output
    type: text
    example: "EPSG:4326"
  distance:
    label: Distance
    description: Some distance measurement (in meters) for a parameter
    type: int
    example: 1000
Specifying an example will auto-fill that input with the example unless changed by the user. If you do not want an example that auto-fills the input, write “example: null”. This will leave the input blank unless the user adds one. Not specifying any example will cause an error. It is mandatory that a script can be run successfully by leaving all the examples and simply pressing Run.
There are several different types of user inputs that can be specified in the YAML file:

Note that the square brackets specify an array, where the user can input multiple values separated by a comma. This is useful if you want the analysis to run with several different parameters (e.g. for multiple species or with multiple raster bands).

The user inputs can also be file types if you want to upload a file or connect the script to a previous one that outputs a specific file type. There are several file types that you can specify:

For example:
inputs:
  landcover_raster:
    label: Raster of landcover
    description: Landcover data pulled from EarthEnv database with 1x1km resolution
    type: application/geo+json
    example: null
  species_occurences:
    label: Occurence points of species
    description: Occurence points from GBIF or uploaded by the user
    type: text/csv
    example: null
The input type can also be set to a limited number of keywords that will automatically generate standardized selectors adapted for the input type. For example, specifying ‘country’ as input type will create a dropdown menu with a standardized list of countries from GeoNames. Selecting ‘crsBbox’ will allow the user to define a bounding box from a country or by clicking on a map. Here is the current list of available selectors:



Input name
Description





country
Creates a selector (drop down menu) with a standardized list of countries. GeoNames is used as the reference for the country list.



countryRegion
Creates a selector (drop down menu) with a standardized list of regions (provinces, states, etc) within a selected country. GeoNames is used as the reference for the list of regions.



countryRegionCRS
Creates a selector (drop down menu) for choosing a coordinate reference system adapted for a specific country and/or region.



CRS
Creates a selector for specifying a coordinate reference system.



crsBbox
Creates a button to open an interface that allows the user to specify a bounding box (geographical minima and maxima) based on an optional selection of country/region and on a CRS, or by clicking on the map to set the bounds of the area of interest for the analysis.

Full location object. Creates a button to open an interface that allows the user to specify a country, region, coordinate reference system and bounding box (geographical minima and maxima)



stac_asset[] | Creates a button to open a STAC catalog browser, where the user picks assets (for example Cloud Optimized GeoTIFF layers) from one or more collections. The script receives a list of selections. See STAC assets. | |





Note that the use of these selectors will create objects that contain multiple elements. For example, the country selector will create an input object that contains the country name in English, the ISO3 code of the country, the ISO2 code, as well as the bounding box of that country, in longitude, latitude coordinates. See the full list of those keys for each selector here.

Here is an example output:
outputs:

    label: Analysis result
    description: The result of the analysis, in CSV form
    type: text/csv
  result_plot:
    label: Result plot
    description: Plot of results

Specifying R and Python package dependencies with conda
“Conda provides package, dependency, and environment management for any language.” If a script is dependent on a specific package version, conda will load that package version to prevent breaking changes when packages are updated. BON in a Box uses a central conda environment that includes commonly used libraries, and supports dedicated environments for the scripts that need it.
This means that instead of installing packages during script execution scripts, they are installed in the R environment in conda. Note that you still need to load the packages in your scripts using the library() command for R or import for Python.

Check if the libraries you need are in conda
To check if the packages you need are already in the default conda environment, go to runners/conda/r-environment.yml or runners/conda/python-environment.yml in the BON in a Box project folder. The list of packages already installed can be found under “dependencies”.
If all the packages that you need are in the R environment file and you do not need specific package versions, you do not need to specify a conda sub environment and you can skip the next step.


Specify a conda sub-environment in your YML file
If you include a conda section, make sure you list all your dependencies. If you specify a conda environment in your YML file, it is creating a new separate conda environment, not a supplement to the base environment. This means that all of the packages that you need for the script need to be specified here, even if they are in the r-environment.yml file.
Search for your package names on anaconda. Packages that are in anaconda will be recognized by conda and can be included in the conda sub-environment in the YML file. If your package is not there, see below.

RPythonJulia


Note that every conda sub environment and script in R must load rjson because it is necessary for running the pipelines in BON in a Box
Example of conda sub-environment for an R script:
conda: # Optional: if you script requires specific versions of packages.
  channels:
    - conda-forge # make sure to put conda forge first
    # - r # use this chanel only if some packages are not available in conda-forge
  dependencies:
    - r-rjson # read inputs and save outputs for R scripts
    - r-terra
    - r-ggplot2
    - r-rredlist=1.0.0 # package=version


Example of conda sub-environment for a python script. You do not need to put anything after conda-forge or before the package names when specifying a conda environment for python.
conda:
  channels:
    - conda-forge
  dependencies:
    - openeo
    - pandas


Conda dependency management is not available in Julia. There is a central project at /julia_depot/. To install packages, use biab_ensure_package(["Pkg1", "Pkg2"]) at the top of your script, which holds back concurrent scripts during installation. Packages added this way are not version-pinned and are shared by all scripts using the central project.
For reproducible and isolated dependencies, place a Project.toml and its Manifest.toml in the same folder as your script. The script then runs in its own environment, created from these files. You can generate them by running the script once and copying the Project.toml and Manifest.toml found in its output folder.



For more information, refer to the conda documentation.


Loading packages that are not available in conda
If you need a package that is not available in conda, such as one downloaded from GitHub, install the package directly in the script. Do not add these packages to the conda portion of the yml file because conda will not be able to recognize them.
In R, concurrent installation of packages can be problematic (for example when running the same script multiple times in parallel). For this language only, you must use the function `biab_ensure_package(…)` that monitors the R locking mechanism to hold back the concurrent scripts during installation. Below is an example usage:

biab_ensure_package(
    "duckdbfs",
    version = "0.1.2",
    installer = function() {
        remotes::install_version("duckdbfs", version = "0.1.2", dependencies = FALSE, upgrade = "never")
    }
)

biab_ensure_package(
    "duckspatial",
    version = "0.9.0",
    installer = function() {
        remotes::install_github("Cidree/duckspatial@v0.9.0", dependencies = FALSE, upgrade = "never")
    }
)

library(duckdbfs)
library(duckspatial)

Full example of a YAML file:
script: script_name.R
name: Script Name
description: Describe what the script does
author:
  - name: John Doe
    email: john.doe@example.com
  - name: Jane Doe
    email: jane.doe@example.com
    identifier: https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000
    role: Software, Visualization, Conceptualization
reviewer:
  - name: John Smith
    email: john.smith@example.com
  - name: Jane Smith
    email: jane.smith@example.com
    identifier: https://orcid.org/0000-0000-0000-0000
inputs:
  landcover_raster:
    label: Raster of landcover
    description: Landcover data pulled from EarthEnv database with 1x1km resolution
    type: application/geo+json
  crs:
    label: coordinate reference system for output
    description: ESPG coordinate reference system for output
    type: int
    example: 4326
  unit_distance:
    label: unit for distance measurement
    description: String value of
    type: options
    options:
      - "m2"
      - "km2"
outputs:
  result:
    label: Analysis result
    description: The result of the analysis, in CSV form
    type: text/csv
  result_plot:
    label: Result plot
    description: Plot of results
    type: image/png
conda: # Optional, only needed if you need packages not in the central environment
  channels:
    - conda-forge
    - r
  dependencies:
    - r-rjson=0.2.22 #package=version
    - r-rredlist
    - r-ggplot2
    - r-sf
    - r-terra
compute: # Optional, specify compute requirements for kubernetes or HPC clusters. If absent, default values apply.
  hpc: false # Optional, send to a HPC cluster if available. Defaults to false.
  mem: 4Gi # Cap for the memory usage, default 4Gi.
  mem-max: 64Gi # Optional, if the job fails with OOM, the job's available memory will be increased up to this value.
  cpus-per-task: 4 # Number of CPU  allocated, default 4.
  time: "02:00:00" # Only when "hpc: true", maximum time allowed before the job is interrupted.
YAML is a space sensitive format, so make sure all the tab sets are correct in the file.
If inputs are outputs from a previous step in the pipeline, make sure to give the inputs and outputs the same name and they will be automatically linked in the pipeline.

    email: # Optional, email address of the author. This will be publicly available
    identifier: # Optional, full URL of a unique digital identifier, such as an ORCID.
    role: # Optional, string with roles undertaken by the author in their contribution. We recommend to use CRediT roles (https://credit.niso.org/).

    label:
    description:
    type:
    example: # optional, for documentation purpose only

references: # 0 to many
  - text: # plain text reference
    link: # full link to the resource (ex. https://doi.org/...)

section: Step 4: Integrating YAML inputs and outputs into your script
text:
Step 4: Integrating YAML inputs and outputs into your script
Now that you have created your YAML file, the inputs and outputs need to be integrated into your scripts.
The scripts perform the actual work behind the scenes. They are located in /scripts folder
Currently supported versions of R, Julia, Python and shell are displayed in the server info tab of the user interface.
Script life cycle:

Script launched with output folder as a parameter (In R, an outputFolder variable in the R session. In Julia, Shell and Python, the output folder is received as an argument.)
Script reads input.json to get execution parameters (ex. species, area, data source, etc.)
Script performs its task
Script generates output.json containing links to result files, or native values (ex. number, string, etc.)

See empty R script for a minimal script life cycle example.

Receiving inputs
When running a script, a folder is created for each given set of parameters. The same parameters result in the same folder, different parameters result in a different folder. The inputs for a given script are saved in a generated input.json file in this unique run folder.
This file contains the id of the parameters that were specified in the yaml script description, associated to the values for this run. Example:
{
    "fc": ["L", "LQ", "LQH"],
    "method_select_params": "AUC",
    "n_folds": 2,
    "orientation_block": "lat_lon",
    "partition_type": "block",
    "predictors": [
        "/output/data/loadFromStac/6af2ccfcd4b0ffe243ff01e3b7eccdc3/bio1_75548ca61981-01-01.tif",
        "/output/data/loadFromStac/6af2ccfcd4b0ffe243ff01e3b7eccdc3/bio2_7333b3d111981-01-01.tif"
    ],
    "presence_background": "/output/SDM/setupDataSdm/edb9492031df9e063a5ec5c325bacdb1/presence_background.tsv",
    "proj": "EPSG:6622",
    "rm": [0.5, 1.0, 2.0]
}
The script reads the input.json file that is in the run folder. This JSON file is automatically created from the BON in a Box pipeline.

RPythonJulia


A convenience function biab_inputs is loaded in R by default to load the file into a list. Here is an example of how to read the input file in the R script:
input <- biab_inputs()
Next, for any functions that are using these inputs, they need to be specified.
Inputs are specified by input$input_name.
For example, to create a function to take the square root of a number that was input by the user in the UI:
result <- sqrt(input$number)
This means if the user inputs the number 144, this will be run in the function and output 12.
Here is another example to read in an output from a previous step of the pipeline, which was output in csv format.
dat <- read.csv(input$csv_file)
The input that is specified in the script needs to match the name that is in the YML file. For example, to load the landcover rasters that I used as an example above, I would write:
landcover <- rast(input$landcover_raster)
And to project it using the CRS that the user specified:
landcover_projected <- project(landcover, input$crs)
When the inputs were entered through preset selectors, the values associated with the selected options are available as a list with values described here. For example, to access the bounding box of an selector with name study_area_bbox of type crsBbox. The bounding box can be accessed through:
bbox <- input$study_area_bbox$bbox
and the ID of the coordinate reference system of the bounding box, made of the authority and code:
crs_id <- paste0(input$study_area_bbox$CRS$authority,input$study_area_bbox$CRS$code)


A convenience function biab_inputs is loaded in Python by default to load the file into a list. Here is an example of how to read the input file in the script and use it’s value:
data = biab_inputs()
my_int = data['some_int_input']
# do something with my_int
To access selector values in Python, the approach is similar to R. For example, to create the CRS ID from the authority and code:
crs_id = data['study_area_bbox']['CRS']['authority']+':'+str(data['study_area_bbox']['CRS']['code'])


The following code allows to read inputs from the json file into a variable in a julia script:
using JSON

# Read the inputs from input.json
input_data = open("input.json", "r") do f
    JSON.parse(f)
end

number = input_data["number"]
# do something with number
To access selector values in Julia, the approach is similar to R or Python. For example, to create the CRS ID from the authority and code:
crs_id = string(input_data["study_area_bbox"]["CRS"]["authority"],":",input_data["study_area_bbox"]["CRS"]["code"])





Writing outputs
The outputs can be saved in a variety of file formats or primitive values (int, text, etc.). The format must be accurately specified in the YAML file. If your script has many outputs, it is recommended to call biab_output(...) throughout your script, and not only at the end: in the event that your script fails, the results that had already been already output can be valuable to understand what has happened.

RPythonJulia


A variable named outputFolder is automatically loaded and contains the file path to output folder.
In R, a convenience function biab_output allows to save the outputs. Here is an example of an output with a csv file and a plot in png format.
result_path <- file.path(outputFolder, "result.csv")
write.csv(result, result_path, row.names = F )
biab_output("result", result_path)

result_plot_path <- file.path(outputFolder, "result_plot.png")
ggsave(result_path, result)
biab_output("result_plot", result_plot_path)


A variable named output_folder is automatically loaded and contains the file path to output folder.
A convenience function biab_output allows to save the outputs as soon as they are created in the course of your script.
intOutput = 12345
biab_output("my_int_output", intOutput)


A variable named output_folder is loaded before your script is executed. It contains a string representation of the output folder.
A convenience function biab_output allow to save the outputs as soon as they are created in the course of your script.
# Write the output file to disk
my_output_path=joinpath(output_folder, "someOutput.csv")
open(my_output_path, "w") do f
    write(f, #= ... =#)
end

# Add it to the BON in a Box outputs for this script
biab_output("my_output", my_output_path)





Modifying your script
When modifying scripts in the /scripts folder, servers do not need to be restarted:

When modifying an existing script, simply save the file and re-run the script from the UI for the new version to be executed.
When adding or renaming scripts, refresh the browser page.
If your scripts depends on additional files or external dependencies that have been updated, the update will not be detected automatically. In that case, re-save the main script file - the one reference in the .yml file - to trigger a re-execution for the next runs (we use the saved date of the script file to trigger re-runs).

When modifying pipelines in the /pipelines folder, servers do not need to be restarted:

In the pipeline editor, click save and run it again from the “pipeline run” page.
When adding or renaming pipelines, refresh the browser page.



Script validation
The syntax and structure of the script description file will be validated on push. To run the validation locally, run validate.sh in your terminal.
This validates that the syntax and structure are correct, but not that it’s content is correct. Hence, peer review of the scripts and the description files is mandatory before accepting a pull requests. Accepted pipelines are tagged as in development, in review, reviewed or deprecated with an optional message describing why it was given that status. Scripts that are not intended for real-world use cases are tagged as examples.


Reporting problems
The output keys info, warning and error can be used to report problems in script execution. They do not need to be described in the outputs section of the description. They will be displayed with special formatting in the UI, and markdown can be used to emphasize or link to debugging resources.
Any error message will also halt the script and the rest of the pipeline. It is recommended to output specific error messages to avoid crashes when errors can be foreseen. This can be done using the biab_error_stop helper function, or by writing an “error” attribute to the output.json file.
For example, if an analysis should stop if the result was less than 0:

RPythonJulia


# R helper function for errors
# stop if result is less than 0
if (result < 0){
    biab_error_stop("Analysis was halted because result is less than 0.")
    # Script stops here
}

# Other reporting functions
biab_warning("This warning will appear in the UI, but does not stop the pipeline.")
biab_info("This message will appear in the UI.")


if result < 0 :
  biab_error_stop("Analysis was halted because result is less than 0.")
  # Script stops here

# Other reporting functions
biab_warning("This warning will appear in the UI, but does not stop the pipeline.")
biab_info("This message will appear in the UI.")


# Sanitize the inputs
if result < 0
    biab_error_stop("Analysis was halted because result is less than 0.")
    # Script stops here
end

# Other reporting functions
biab_warning("This warning will appear in the UI, but does not stop the pipeline.")
biab_info("This message will appear in the UI.")



And then the customized message will appear in the UI.
A crash will have the same behavior as an error output, stopping the pipeline with the error displayed in the UI. A script that completed without creating the output.json file is assumed to have crashed, and a general error message will be displayed. In both cases, the logs can be inspected for more details.

Step 5: Testing your script
To start testing:

Connect to the server by running ./server-up.sh in a Linux terminal (e.g. Git Bash or WSL on Windows or Terminal on Mac). Make sure you are in the bon-in-a-box-pipeline directory on your computer.
In a web browser, type http://localhost/.

You can test your script in the “run script” tab of the tool. This will generate a form where you can enter sample inputs or use your default parameters to run the script for debugging.
